extracted.intended_audience: regulated industry (power plant developers/operators and manufacturers), state regulators, environmental lawyers, and stakeholders submitting comments to EPA
extracted.subtask_short: BSER determination for new combustion turbines
extracted.subtask_description: EPA's CAA section 111(b) preamble establishing the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and multi-phase standards of performance for new and reconstructed combined cycle (base load and intermediate load) combustion turbine EGUs, evaluating technologies (highly efficient generation, CCS, hydrogen co-firing) against statutory criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately Demonstrated — Highly Efficient Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA proposed and is finalizing that highly efficient combined cycle designs are adequately demonstrated because highly efficient combined cycle EGUs have been demonstrated by multiple facilities for decades, and the efficiency improvements of the most efficient designs are incremental in nature and do not change in any significant way how the combustion turbine is operated or maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less stringent standards are used for smaller base load turbines (<2,000 MMBtu/h) due to HRSG efficiency differences. The EPA treats efficient generation as commercially available and achievable because many recently constructed combustion turbines have achieved the proposed efficiency levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs — Highly Efficient Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the base load subcategory, the EPA considers the cost of high-efficiency combined cycle EGUs to be reasonable: capital costs ~1.9% higher than standard efficiency combined cycle EGUs while fuel use is ~2.6% lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's lifecycle analysis: fuel-cost reductions fully offset capital costs at capacity factors ≥40% over a 30‑year facility life, so BSER based on high-efficiency combined cycle turbines would have minimal, if any, overall compliance costs because capital is recovered through reduced fuel costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Air Quality Health and Environmental Impacts and Energy Requirements — Highly Efficient Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of highly efficient generation reduces all non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements compared to less efficient generation because less fuel is required for the same output, reducing emissions of all pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finds no adverse effects on energy requirements; nationwide impacts on electricity supply, prices, or sector structure would not be significant because technology does not add substantial costs and some costs are offset by fuel savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Reductions in CO2 Emissions — Highly Efficient Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined the standard of performance reflecting this BSER is 800 lb CO2/MWh‑gross for base load combustion turbines and estimated associated annual CO2 and NOX reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: EPA reviewed recently constructed combined cycle EGUs (2015–2022), adjusted any units above 800 lb CO2/MWh‑gross down to 800 while holding average capacity factor, summed reductions, divided by years evaluated to estimate annual reductions (initial estimate: 313,000 tons CO2 and 23 tons NOX; year 3: 939,000 tons CO2 and 69 tons NOX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of Development and Implementation of Technology — Highly Efficient Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining highly efficient turbines as part of the BSER will advance penetration of best-performing turbines and incentivize manufacturers to offer improved turbines that meet standards of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor supports selecting the technology as BSER but EPA states highly efficient generation qualifies as BSER even without relying on this promotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and Permissibility of a Multi-Part (Phased) BSER and Standard of Performance
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b) authorizes the EPA to promulgate standards of performance based on a BSER that is a set of controls with multiple components and to set phased standards that become effective upon promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phased approach: affected sources are legally subject upon promulgation, must comply with phase 1 (first component) upon startup and with phase 2 (first+second components) by specified future date (e.g., Jan 2032). D.C. Circuit caselaw allows adequate demonstration to accommodate 'lead time.' EPA cites prior rulemakings with phased/stepped compliance to support reasonableness of lead time.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER Determination — First Component for Base Load: Highly Efficient Generation + Best O&M
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing that highly efficient generating technology in combination with the best operating and maintenance practices is the first component of the BSER for base load combustion turbines; phase‑1 standards are based on this application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of basis: qualifies because it is adequately demonstrated, implementable at reasonable cost, achieves emission reductions, and does not have significant adverse non‑air quality health/environmental impacts or energy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower‑Emitting Fuels and Hydrogen Co‑Firing — Consideration but Not Finalized
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered lower‑emitting fuels and co‑firing low‑GHG hydrogen as potential BSER components but did not propose or finalize lower‑emitting fuels as the second component for intermediate or base load because they would achieve few emission reductions compared to highly efficient generation with or without CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not determined to be BSER for base or intermediate load, the standard is technology neutral so affected sources may comply by co‑firing hydrogen if they choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS with 90% Capture — Overview as a BSER Component
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA explains CCS with 90% capture is a component of the BSER for new base load combustion turbines because it can be applied at the stack, achieves substantial emission reductions, can capture and permanently sequester at least 90% of CO2, is adequately demonstrated at scale and is widely applicable, and there are substantial sequestration opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's balancing: CCS costs are reasonable given cost declines and policy incentives (e.g., IRC section 45Q), non‑air quality impacts can be mitigated, energy requirements are not unreasonably adverse, and CCS designation would promote further development and deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately Demonstrated — Legal Test Applied to CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standard: the 'system' must be adequately demonstrated and the 'standard' must be achievable; an achievable standard is one where sufficient evidence shows affected sources can adopt the system to achieve the required limitation. EPA may extrapolate from one source type to a similar source (Lignite Energy Council v. EPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concludes amine post‑combustion CO2 capture (used on coal units) and other evidence show that 90% capture is adequately demonstrated and achievable for natural gas combined cycle EGUs, noting differences in flue gas composition do not preclude achieving 90% capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 Capture Technologies Applicable to Combined Cycle Turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: New combustion turbines can use amine‑based post‑combustion capture or oxy‑combustion (e.g., NET Power Allam‑Fetvedt Cycle); post‑combustion systems require cooled flue gas (HRSG) and correct sizing/design to handle lower CO2 concentrations in NGCC flue gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes capture from dilute CO2 streams (3–4 vol% for NGCC vs ~13–15% for coal) is more challenging but commercially available amine solvents can achieve 90% capture; HRSG cooling is energy‑efficient for cooling prior to capture equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/Project Evidence Supporting CCS Adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cites multiple demonstration and commercial projects (e.g., Bellingham Energy Center capture 85–95% on a slipstream, Technology Centre Mongstad, Peterhead planning, NET Power demonstrations, Sutter, Deer Park, Baytown projects) and vendor statements (Fluor Econamine FG Plus, Shell CANSOLV, MHI solvents) as evidence that CCS at ≥90% capture is demonstrated or in development for NGCC/combine cycle units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details used as support: Bellingham logged 120,000+ hours and 98.5% availability on a 40 MW slipstream; vendors and international pilot/commercial projects achieving >95% capture; DOE‑assisted and permit‑documented projects in planning and FEED stages; these corroborate adequacy and commercial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and Sequestration Components of CCS — Adequacy and Siting Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's analysis of CO2 transport and geologic storage for CCS on combined cycle turbines parallels its analysis for coal units; transport and sequestration are adequately demonstrated and there are vast sequestration opportunities across the continental U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes access to transport and storage sites may influence where new sources are sited and expects developers have considered likely regulatory regimes; EPA incorporates prior discussions of capture, transport, and sequestration in its overall BSER finding.
